title: Mini nutritional assessment and mortality after hip fracture surgery in the elderly
journal: The Journal of Nutrition, Health & Aging

sections.abstract:
Hip fracture surgery in elderly patients is associated with a poor postoperative outcome and a high mortality. Malnutrition is a frequent problem in elderly patients and may be associated with mortality after hip fracture surgery. The Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) is a valuable tool to identify malnourished patients and those at risk for malnutrition.

To evaluate the association between the preoperative MNA score and mortality after surgery for hip fractures in elderly patients.

Patients with a hip fracture and an indication for surgery were included in our study. This study was part of a randomized trial on the effect of taurine on postoperative outcome in elderly hip fracture patients. The MNA was assessed on admission before surgery. Length of stay, postoperative complications and mortality were documented. The association of the MNA score on postoperative outcome and mortality was analyzed using Cox regression analysis.

The one-year survival rate in 226 elderly hip fracture patients was 79%. In-hospital mortality rates and 1-year mortality were 27% and 46% in malnourished patients, 12% and 26% in patients at risk for malnutrition and 7% and 17% in well-nourished patients as assessed by MNA.

Preoperative malnutrition measured by the MNA is associated with mortality in elderly hip fracture patients.
sections.introduction:
Hip fractures are common in the growing elderly population worldwide and pose a serious healthcare problem. In the year 2000, the incidence of hip fractures was 1.6 million worldwide and is estimated to grow to 6.3 million in 2050 ( 1 , 2 ). Accounting for only 14% of all fractures, the health care costs of hip fractures are extremely high making up a 72% of the total fracture related costs ( 3 , 4 ).

Elderly people have a high risk for hip fractures due to an increased tendency to fall in the presence of osteoporosis. Reduced muscle mass, impaired gait, balance and sight problems and medication use contribute to the risk of falling ( 5 ). After hip fracture surgery elderly patients have a poor postoperative outcome and age adjusted mortality rates are high ( 6 ). The one-year mortality rate after hip surgery ranges from 10 to 27 percent ( 7 , 8 , 9 ). Patient characteristics that are risk factors for a poor postoperative outcome and an increased mortality risk include advanced age, male gender, high American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) classification, delirium, thromboembolic events, co-morbidities, poor nutritional state and poor mental state ( 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ). Most of these items indentify risk factors that are difficult or impossible to change for the better. In contrast, a poor nutritional status may be improved by targeted community based nutritional therapy ( 14 ). However, the malnourished elderly patient is not easily identified using traditional anthropometric measurements, such as weight or body mass index (BMI).

A valuable tool to better identify malnourishment or risk for malnourishment in elderly patients is the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA). The MNA is composed of a screening part and an assessment part. The screening part consists of questions about food intake, weight loss, mobility, stress, neuropsychological problems and body mass index (BMI). The assessment part consists of more detailed questions about food intake, the self view of nutritional and health status and measurements of mid-arm and calf circumference ( 15 ). At this moment, there is not yet much evidence to support the predictive value of MNA in hip surgery patients.

The aim of our study was to evaluate the association of preoperative MNA score on postoperative mortality after hip fracture surgery in elderly patients.
sections.methods:
This retrospective cohort study was part of a double blind, randomized, placebo-controlled intervention study on the effect of perioperative administration of taurine versus a placebo in elderly patients qualified for hip surgery. The local ethics committee approved this study protocol ( 16 ). Written informed consent was granted for all patients prior to participation. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT00497978 .

Patients in this study presented with a hip fracture between March 2008 and July 2010 at the Medical Center Alkmaar or the Red Cross Hospital, Beverwijk, the Netherlands. All patients with the age of 75 years or older and an indication for hip surgery were selected for this study. Patients were treated with hemi-arthroplasty or open reduction internal fixation (ORIF). The surgeon decided which surgical procedure was applied, depending on the type and dislocation of the fracture. Patients without a preoperative MNA score or insufficient data on the outcomes measures were excluded.

Nutritional status was assessed before surgery with the complete MNA, i.e. the MNA screening- and assessment part. The screening part consists of questions about food intake, weight loss, mobility, stress, neuropsychological problems and body mass index (BMI). The assessment part consists of more detailed questions about food intake, the self view of nutritional and health status and measurements of mid-arm and calf circumference. In our study, the clinical researcher or a trained nurse assessed the MNA. It takes less than 10 minutes to assess the MNA. In patients with cognitive impairment, there always were relatives or friends to help out with the questionnaire. Malnourished patients were defined as having a MNA score less than 17 points, for risk for malnutrition the MNA score was between 17 and 23.5 points and well nourished patients had a MNA score above 23.5 points.

After surgery, postoperative complications and mortality were documented. Postoperative complications were categorized as infectious and cardiovascular complications. We monitored the patients from the day of submission until the day of hospital discharged. After hospital discharged, we monitored mortality every three months until a year, counted from the day of surgery.

Since this study reports data from an interventional trial possible differences between the intervention and control group with respect to patient and surgical characteristics and postoperative outcomes were tested. Taurine had no effect on the variables measured in the present study. For this reason the data of the taurine and control group were pooled and analyzed as one group.

Nominal and ordinal variables were described as numbers with percentages. Continuous variables were described as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges. Between group differences were tested using the chi-square test for nominal and categorical variables. For continuous variables ANOVA was used. A significance level of 5% was used.

The association of patients' preoperative nutritional status with postoperative in hospital and 1 year mortality was analysed using logistic and Cox regression analyses respectively. The strength of the associations was reported as Odds and Hazard ratio's (OR and HR) respectively, both with 95% Confidence Intervals (95%CI). In multivariable analyses both estimates were corrected for confounding effects of age and sex resulting in adjusted OR's and HR's. One-year survival was visualised by a Kaplan Meier plot. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, version 20, 2009, Chicago, IL, USA).
sections.results:
In total, 236 patients presented with a hip fracture with an indication for surgery. Surgery was performed between March 2008 and July 2010 at the Medical Center Alkmaar and the Red Cross Hospital, Beverwijk, the Netherlands. In total, 226 patients (165 female and 61 male) had pre-operative MNA score as well as sufficient information on the outcome measures and were included in the study. There were no differences in the type of surgical procedures or general patient characteristics between the MNA groups; results are shown in Table 1 . Patient- and surgery characteristics

Preoperative nutritional status was assessed in 226 patients using the total MNA, i.e. the screening- and the assessment part. In total, 11 patients (5%) had a MNA below 17 points indicating malnourishment, 60 patients (27%) had a MNA between 17 and 23.5 indicating the risk of malnourishment and 155 patients (68%) had a MNA above 23.5 points indicating a good nutritional status.

No differences in postoperative complications were noted; results are shown in Table 2 . Significantly higher in-hospital and 1 year mortality rates were found in the MNA < 17 group versus MNA 17 – 23.5 and MNA > 23.5. Taking the wellnourished category as reference logistic regression analysis showed that a MNA score < 17 was significantly associated with in-hospital mortality. After adjustment for age and sex the association just lost significance. Using the same reference category cox regression analysis showed a significant association between a MNA score < 17 and 1-year mortality that remained significant after adjustment. Furthermore, we performed an additional Cox regression analysis with all patients who were discharged from the hospital. Comparing the well-nourished patients, the HR's are 2.5 and 1.6 for the malnourished patients and patients at risk for malnutrition, respectively. In conclusion, if we exclude patients who died in the hospital, the HR's remain more or less the same, but are not significant anymore. Table 3 shows an overview of “In hospital mortality” and “1 year survival” in different MNA categories. Figure 1 shows the Kaplan Meier curve for 1-year survival. sections.discussion:
In the largest study to date we showed that preoperative MNA is associated with mortality after hip surgery in elderly patients. The overall in hospital mortality in our study was 9%. The overall one-year survival rate in our study was 79%. The greater part of the deceased patients died in hospital, this reflects the high impact of surgery in the short-term. This is consistent with results from other studies.( 7 , 8 , 9 ) Malnourished patients had lower survival rates compared to patients at risk for malnutrition or well-nourished patients. One year after surgery, malnourished patients have an increased mortality risk, which reflects the high impact of a hip fracture in this fragile population.

Since improvement of nutritional status of patients takes more than the approximately 5-7 days of their hospital submission, possible intervention should focus on the rehabilitation period after their hospital admission. That is the period that gains can be achieved. More attention on nutritional status should be paid in rehabilitation centers and nursing homes. However, if patients are seriously malnourished, in hospital nutritional intervention should be considered. In addition, patients and their family should be better informed about the in hospital risks and the one-year mortality rate after hip fracture surgery. If patients are more aware of their risks, they are more prone to nutritional intervention.

Several studies ( 5 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ) investigated the predictive value of nutritional status on postoperative outcome after surgery for hip fractures. The majority of these studies used preoperative albumin levels as an indicator for nutritional status. In general, they found an association between preoperative albumin levels and postoperative outcome after hip surgery (5, 19, 21-24). Of these, three studies used the combination of preoperative albumin levels and total lymphocyte count (TLC) as indicators for nutritional status and also found a strong association with postoperative outcome (21, 22, 24). In addition, a recent systematic review revealed only two preoperative parameters to predict postoperative outcome in elderly general surgery patients: weight loss and serum albumin ( 26 ). However, levels of albumin and TLC are influenced by inflammatory state and underlying disease and do not reflect nutritional status per se.

The MNA is a valuable diagnostic tool to identify elderly patients that are malnourished or at risk for malnutrition. Furthermore, it is widely used to predict prognosis and outcome in different diseases ( 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ). Recently, two studies focused on the association with MNA and postoperative outcome in hip surgery patients. Guo et al. ( 18 ) found an association between preoperative low MNA score and wound healing after hip surgery. In addition, Gumiero et al. ( 17 ) found an association between preoperative MNA and six-month mortality in 88 hip fracture surgical patients. Our larger study confirms the value of preoperative assessment of MNA. The MNA is able to distinguish between risk for malnutrition and malnutrition and thereby provides possibilities for early interventions in a fragile population.

Although the relation with preoperative nutritional status and postoperative outcome is shown in different studies, it is not the only factor that influences fracture healing and postoperative outcome. In addition, elderly with a poor nutritional status often have underlying comorbidity or cognitive problems. However, nutritional status is an important factor in outcome and can be improved and thereby we think that is important to know the nutritional status prior to surgery.

Several studies investigated the effect of intervention studies on postoperative outcome after hip fracture surgery. Although the evidence is scarce, it seems that nutritional interventions improves postoperative outcome after hip fracture surgery and reduces postoperative complications ( 32 , 33 , 34 ).

We acknowledge that our study has several limitations. First, the number of patients that were malnourished was relatively small compared to patients at risk for malnutrition and wellnourished patients. Second, we excluded 10 patients without a preoperative MNA or insufficient outcome data. Potentially, this creates the risk for selection bias.

In our opinion, it should be a standard procedure to assess the MNA in elderly patients admitted to the hospital with a hip fracture and an indication for surgery. The preoperative MNA may be used as a possible tool in predicting outcome but also identifies malnourished patients and patients at risk for malnutrition. This helps to direct targeted interventions to improve nutritional status and thereby improve postoperative outcome and postoperative mortality.

Several studies ( 35 , 36 , 37 ) investigated the effect of nutritional interventions in elderly hip fracture patients. In general, these intervention studies showed positive effects on nutritional status, postoperative outcome and quality of life after surgery. Future research should focus on nutritional interventions in elderly hip fracture patients in order to improve the postoperative outcome and one-year mortality.

In conclusion, our study showed that the MNA is a valuable tool in assessing malnutrition related mortality after surgery for hip fracture in elderly patients. In our opinion, the MNA could be conducted in all elderly patients with hip fractures in order to identify malnutrition directing targeted nutritional interventions to improve postoperative outcome.
